a: Levi dreamed
p: The Testament of Levi tells the same dream: Levi is clothed as priest at Bethel.
b: The Testament of Levi 8, a Greek work that drew on older Levi traditions, has the same scene, as Charles shows: at Bethel seven men in white tell Levi to put on "the robe of the priesthood" and say that from now on he and his descendants will be priests of the Lord forever. Its chapter 9 adds that Jacob too had the dream and tithed everything through Levi. Jubilees gives only the bare report of the dream, but the two works clearly share one story of how Levi became a priest before Aaron.
r: Testament of Levi 8; Testament of Levi 9; 30:18–20

a: a priest of God Most High
p: Melchizedek's title in Genesis 14, given here to Levi. The Hasmonean priest-kings used it too.
b: Only Melchizedek is called "a priest of God Most High" in Genesis 14:18. Jubilees gives the title to Levi and, in the next verse, borrows Genesis 14:20, "a tenth of everything." Charles noted that this was the title of the Hasmonean high priests: Josephus quotes a decree of Augustus that speaks of "Hyrcanus the high priest of the Almighty God" (Antiquities 16.6.2, Whiston's English; Charles gives the Greek as "high priest of the Most High God"). Charles read the verse as support for the Hasmonean priest-kings, who claimed Melchizedek's title for Levi's line.

a: He set aside a tenth of everything that had come with him
p: At Bethel Jacob had promised God a tenth of everything. Here he pays it, people included.
b: Genesis 28:22 ends Jacob's vow: "of everything you give me I will give a tenth, a tenth to you." Genesis never tells how he paid it. Jubilees does, and makes the tenth cover even people, which leads to Levi, the tenth son, given to God (32:3). The Testament of Levi 9 says Jacob "rising early" tithed everything through Levi, close to this verse.

a: the count went up and came down on Levi
p: Counted backward from the unborn Benjamin, Levi is the tenth son: God's tenth.
b: Counting the sons in the order of their births in Genesis 29–30 and 35, but from the youngest upward (Benjamin, still in the womb, then Joseph, Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, Gad, Naphtali, Dan, Judah), Levi comes tenth. So the tenth of Jacob's sons falls to God. The Byzantine chroniclers George Syncellus and George Cedrenus knew this reckoning, as Charles shows: Syncellus says Levi, "being the tenth from the last," was tithed to God and made high priest. A later Jewish retelling, Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 37, makes Levi the tenth by a different count (Charles).
orig: ወዐርገ ፡ ወወረደ ፡ ላዕሌሁ ፡ ለሌዊ (wäʿärgä wäwärädä laʿlehu lälewi)

a: filled his hands
p: The old Hebrew phrase for making someone a priest, kept word for word in the Ge'ez.
b: Exodus uses the same phrase for Aaron and his sons: "Anoint them, fill their hands, and set them apart" (Exodus 28:41; compare Exodus 29:9). It probably comes from putting the first offerings into the new priest's hands. The Ge'ez keeps the Hebrew idiom, one sign that Jubilees was translated from Hebrew.

a: His father dressed him in the clothes of the priesthood
p: In the 66 books the priesthood begins with Aaron at Sinai. Here Jacob ordains Levi.
b: Goes beyond: Exodus gives the priesthood to Aaron and his sons at Sinai (Exodus 28–29), and Numbers sets the whole tribe of Levi apart later (Numbers 3; 18). Genesis knows no priest in Jacob's family. Jubilees moves the beginning back to Bethel, so that the priests of the Second Temple could say their office was older than Moses. Differs: Hebrews 7:9–10 also places Levi in Genesis, but the other way round: Levi "has been made to give a tenth through Abraham" to Melchizedek, because he was still in his father's body.

a: fourteen bulls from the herd
p: Every number is a multiple of seven, unlike the Feast of Booths in Numbers 29.
b: With the Latin's numbers (see the note on "seven lambs"), the offering is 14, 28, 49, 7 and 21: all sevens, the book's favorite number. The law of Moses sets a different pattern for the Feast of Booths: thirteen bulls on the first day, one fewer each day down to seven, seventy in all, with two rams, fourteen lambs and a goat each day (Numbers 29:12–34). Charles points out the difference. The date, the fifteenth of the seventh month, is the first day of Booths (Leviticus 23:34).

a: the peace offering
p: The Ge'ez says "sacrifice of salvation." Charles calls it a thank-offering.
b: Mäśwaʿtä mädḫanit means "sacrifice of salvation" or "of deliverance." The Plain English Translation renders it "peace offering" across Jubilees (see 21:8): it is the offering whose meat the worshiper and his family eat, as Jacob's household does here (32:7; Leviticus 3; Leviticus 7:11–18). Jacob gives it because God has "rescued him from all his trouble." Charles translates "thank-offering."

a: all the people he gave to him too
t: Claude's theory: why the unclean animals and the people go to Levi
p: Unclean animals and people cannot be sacrificed. In Numbers such tenths and firstborns go to the priest.
b: Claude's suggestion: clean animals can go on the altar, so Jacob burns them. Unclean animals and human beings cannot, so they become Levi's, as in Numbers the firstborn of humans and of unclean animals belong to the priest and must be bought back: "you must buy back the firstborn of humans, and you are to buy back the firstborn of unclean animals" (Numbers 18:15). If so, the Ge'ez needs no "not" (see the variant). Charles took the people as those Levi was to serve as priest. The theory rests on 32:2, 32:8 and Numbers 18:15.

a: out of all his ten brothers
p: Benjamin was not yet born, so Levi had ten brothers, not eleven.
b: Rachel is pregnant with Benjamin (32:3) and gives birth only in 32:33. So at Bethel Levi has ten living brothers. The number fits the book's careful dating, and the picture of one son set apart out of the rest.

a: he set aside a tenth again for the Lord
p: Ge'ez "again a tithe": the second tithe that the next verses explain.
b: The Ge'ez says Jacob "tithed again a tithe" (dagmä ʿaśratä). Charles compares Numbers 18:26, where the Levites give "a tenth of the tithe," but 32:10–14 shows what Jubilees means: a second tenth that the worshiper eats before the Lord, the rule of Deuteronomy 14:22–26.

a: in the place chosen for his name to live there
p: Deuteronomy's phrase for the one sanctuary, here written into the heavenly tablets.
b: Deuteronomy 14:23 says to eat the tithe "before the LORD your God, in the place he will choose to make his name live there." Jubilees takes the rule over almost word for word, but says it was already written on the heavenly tablets in Jacob's day. Charles: "our text holds closely to the law in Deut. xiv. 22 sq."

a: the second tithe
p: Jews of the Second Temple read the law as asking for more than one tithe. Tobit counts them.
b: Numbers 18 gives a tithe to the Levites; Deuteronomy 14 has the worshiper eat a tithe at the sanctuary, and every third year give it to the poor. Many Jews read these as separate tithes. Tobit says he gave a tenth to the sons of Levi and also "set aside the second tenth in money, and every year I went and spent it in Jerusalem" (Tobit 1:7). Jubilees names a "second tithe" too. The Mishnah later gave a whole tractate to it, Ma'aser Sheni ("Second Tithe").

a: Let it be burned in the fire
p: Deuteronomy does not say what to do with an old tithe. Jubilees applies the rule for sacrifices.
b: Goes beyond: the law of the tithe in Deuteronomy 14 sets no time limit. Jubilees borrows the rule for holy meat: "Whatever meat of the sacrifice is left on the third day is to be burned with fire" (Leviticus 7:17), and the Passover rule, "Whatever is left of it until morning, burn in the fire" (Exodus 12:10). Here the limit is a year: each crop is eaten before the next harvest.

a: All the tithe of cattle and sheep
p: The 66 books mention a tithe of animals only in Leviticus 27 and 2 Chronicles 31.
b: "All the tithe of herd and flock ... will be holy to the LORD" (Leviticus 27:32), and Hezekiah's people "brought the tithe of cattle and sheep" (2 Chronicles 31:6). Charles notes that these are the only two places, and that later rabbis read the law more narrowly. Jubilees takes it at its word and gives the animal tithe to the priests.

a: Jacob planned to build up that place
p: Genesis has Jacob promise a house of God at Bethel. Jubilees has an angel stop him building it.
b: Goes beyond, and qualifies: Jacob vowed that his stone "will become a house of God" (Genesis 28:22), and Genesis 35:7 has him build an altar there. Jubilees lets him sacrifice but forbids a lasting sanctuary: "this is not the place" (32:22). In Israel's later history Bethel became Jeroboam's rival shrine: "He placed one calf in Bethel" (1 Kings 12:29). The angel does not name the right place here; the law of 32:10 speaks only of "the place chosen for his name."

a: Your name will not be called only Jacob
p: The Ge'ez adds "only": he keeps both names. Genesis says he will no longer be called Jacob.
b: Genesis 35:10 reads, "Your name will no longer be called Jacob. Israel will be your name." Yet Genesis goes on calling him Jacob. The Ge'ez baḥtito, "alone, only," solves the puzzle: not Jacob only, but Israel too. Jubilees itself keeps using "Jacob." Charles's translation leaves the word out.

a: I am the Lord who made heaven and earth
p: Genesis 35:11 has "I am God Almighty." Jubilees names God as creator.
b: Where Genesis 35:11 reads "I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and become many," Jubilees has God call himself the maker of heaven and earth, the title Melchizedek uses in Genesis 14:19, "maker of heaven and earth." The promise of kings follows Genesis: "kings will come out of your loins."

a: They will judge all the nations as they please.
t: The whole earth, not the land
p: Genesis 35:12 promises the land; Jubilees promises rule over every nation.
b: Goes beyond: in Genesis 35:12 God promises "the land I gave to Abraham and to Isaac." Jubilees widens the gift to "all the earth that is under heaven," and adds rule over all nations. Charles: "our author here forsakes Gen. xxxv. 12." Paul also speaks of a promise that Abraham "would inherit the world" (Romans 4:13), but he means it is received "through the righteousness of faith," not by rule over nations.

a: Jacob watched until he had gone up into heaven
p: Genesis 35:13: "God went up and away from him." Jubilees adds that Jacob watched.
b: Genesis 35:13 says only, "God went up and away from him, at the place where he had spoken with him." Jubilees adds that Jacob watched him go up into heaven, like Manoah and his wife watching the angel go up in the flame (Judges 13:20).

a: seven tablets
p: A lost Jewish book, the Prayer of Joseph, has Jacob say he read the heavenly tablets.
b: Origen quotes the Prayer of Joseph, a lost Jewish writing, in which Jacob says (Greek, as Charles prints it), anegnōn gar en tais plaxi tou ouranou hosa symbēsetai hymin kai tois huiois hymōn, "for I read in the tablets of heaven all that will happen to you and to your sons." Charles thought this verse of Jubilees was its source. Compare the heavenly tablets Enoch reads (1 Enoch 81:1–2); Charles also compares 4 Ezra 14:24.

a: For you will die in peace in Egypt
t: Death in Egypt, burial at home
p: The angel foretells what Genesis 46–50 tells: Jacob dies in Egypt and is buried with his fathers.
b: In Genesis God tells Jacob not to be afraid to go down to Egypt (Genesis 46:3–4), and Jacob asks, "Lay me with my fathers in the cave that is in Ephron the Hittite's field" (Genesis 49:29). His sons do so (Genesis 50:13). Jubilees has the angel reveal all of this at Bethel, years before.

a: Now write it all down
p: In Jubilees the fathers write books, and the books pass down to the priests.
b: Jubilees makes Enoch, Noah and Abraham writers, and here Jacob. Later Jacob gives all his books, and his fathers' books, to Levi to keep and copy (45:16). So the book claims that Israel's priests kept a written law long before Moses. Charles adds that this verse seems to be the source of the Prayer of Joseph (see 32:21).

a: I will bring it all back to your memory
p: Charles compares Jesus' promise that the Spirit will remind the disciples of all he said.
b: Jacob fears he will forget the tablets. The angel promises to remind him. Charles points to John 14:26, where Jesus says that the Advocate "will bring back to your mind all that I told you." In both, a teaching from heaven is kept safe because God himself brings it back to mind.

a: Addition
p: The eighth day of Booths. Its Hebrew name meant an assembly; the Ge'ez name may come from a slip.
b: The day after the seven days of Booths is the "closing assembly" (Leviticus 23:36; Numbers 29:35), Hebrew ʿatseret; 2 Chronicles 7:9 says, "On the eighth day they held a closing gathering." The Ge'ez calls it tosak, "Addition." Charles thought the Ethiopic translator misread a Greek word: the Latin has retentatio, "a keeping back," and Rönsch proposed that Greek epischesis ("holding back") was miscopied epithesis ("adding"). Then Jacob's day would be named because he was held back at Bethel a day longer.

a: the Feast
p: Jews called Booths simply "the Feast," as here.
b: Charles notes that this matches rabbinic usage, where Booths is he-ḥag, "the Feast" (Talmud, Sukkah). John 7 speaks of the same festival and its "last and great day" (John 7:37). Jubilees makes the name, and the extra day, go back to Jacob at Bethel.

a: by the count of the days of the year
p: Charles called this verse "very corrupt" in the Ge'ez and partly corrupt in the Latin.
b: The Ge'ez says the day "goes up into the testimony of the feast days." Charles thought a word for "days" had become "testimony," with the Latin (in dies), and proposed: "its name was called 'a keeping back,' when it was recorded amongst the days of the feast-days in the number of the days of the year." Either way the point is the calendar: the added day is counted into the fixed year of 364 days (6:32).

a: Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died
p: Genesis 35:8 tells the death in one line; Jubilees adds the date and two names.
b: "Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died, and she was buried below Bethel under the oak. So it was named Allon-bacuth" (Genesis 35:8). The Hebrew name means "Oak of Weeping"; Jubilees has "the Oak of Mourning for Deborah" and names the stream as well. Genesis never says that Rebekah herself was with Jacob; Jubilees has her come with him to Bethel and go home after the feast (32:31).

a: Kabratan
p: Genesis 35:16 says Rachel's labor began "some distance" from Ephrath. The Hebrew was read as a name.
b: The Hebrew of Genesis 35:16 has kivrat ha-ʾarets, "a stretch of land," which the site renders "some distance." Charles shows that Jubilees, like the Septuagint's Chabratha, took kivrat as a place name, and so Jacob comes "near the land of Kabratan." It is a small window on how the book was made: from a Hebrew text of Genesis, read word by word.

a: Son of My Pain
p: Genesis 35:18 gives the Hebrew name Ben-oni; Jubilees translates it.
b: "As her life was going out of her, for she was dying, she named him Ben-oni. But his father called him Benjamin" (Genesis 35:18). Ben-oni means "son of my sorrow" or "of my trouble"; the Ge'ez has wäldä ḥəmamyä, "son of my pain." Benjamin means "son of the right hand."

a: Jacob built a standing stone on Rachel's grave
p: Genesis 35:19–20, and Rachel weeping for her children in Jeremiah and Matthew.
b: Genesis says "they buried her on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem," and that the stone "is the standing stone of Rachel's grave to this day" (Genesis 35:19–20). Jubilees says "in the land of Ephrath." Jeremiah later hears "Rachel crying over her children" (Jeremiah 31:15), and Matthew applies the verse to the children of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18).

a: Magdaladraef
p: A run-together form of Genesis 35:21's Migdal-eder, with Ephrath.
b: Genesis 35:21: Israel "pitched his tent beyond Migdal-eder" ("tower of the flock"). Charles explains the Ge'ez name as a compression of "Migdal-Eder Ephrath." The Testament of Reuben 3 sets the same scene "at Gader near Ephrath" (Charles). Micah 4:8 calls Jerusalem "Tower of the Flock."

a: Then he went to his father Isaac, he and his wife Leah
p: Jubilees and the Testament of Reuben both place Reuben's sin while Jacob was away with Isaac.
b: Genesis 35:22 says only that it happened "while Israel was living in that land." Jubilees places it while Jacob and Leah were away visiting Isaac, and so does the Testament of Reuben 3: "for when Jacob our father was absent with Isaac his father," as Charles quotes it. The detail explains how it could happen in Jacob's own camp.

a: Reuben saw Bilhah
t: One verse in Genesis, a whole story here
p: Genesis 35:22 gives the deed in one sentence. Jubilees tells it, and then draws a law from it.
b: "Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel heard" (Genesis 35:22). Goes beyond: Jubilees adds the bath, the night, Bilhah asleep, her cry, and her shame. The Testament of Reuben 3 has the bath too: "if I had not seen Bilhah bathing in a secret place" (Charles). Both make Bilhah innocent, which Genesis does not discuss. The point of the story comes in 33:10–20: the law it illustrates.

a: She pulled back the edge of her covering
p: Ge'ez kənf, "wing, edge," the same image as Deuteronomy's "wing of his father's cloak."
b: The word kənf ("wing") is used for the edge of a covering here and for Bilhah's skirt in 33:7. Hebrew uses the same picture: "He must not lift the wing of his father's cloak" (Deuteronomy 22:30), and Ruth asks Boaz, "Spread the wing of your cloak over your servant" (Ruth 3:9). Lifting a man's "wing" meant taking what belonged to his bed.

a: I am not clean for you
p: Bilhah did nothing wrong, yet she can no longer go to Jacob. Deuteronomy has a similar rule.
b: Matches in idea: a woman who has been with another man may not return to her husband: "her first husband ... may not take her back to be his wife after she has been made unclean" (Deuteronomy 24:4). David shut away the ten concubines Absalom had taken, and "did not go in to them" (2 Samuel 20:3). Goes beyond: Genesis says nothing of Bilhah afterward. Jubilees treats the defilement as real even though she was asleep; the Testament of Reuben 3 says an angel told Jacob (Charles).

a: his father's covering
p: Leviticus' idiom: a father's wife is his "nakedness." The Ge'ez says his "covering."
b: Leviticus 18:8: "Do not expose the nakedness of your father's wife. It is your father's nakedness." The Ge'ez kədnät means a covering or garment, so the idea is that the son strips away what covers his father's honor. In 33:12 the Ge'ez has ḫäfrät, literally "shame," rendered "nakedness" as in Genesis 9:22–23.

a: Jacob never came near her again
p: Genesis has Jacob take the firstborn's place from Reuben for this deed.
b: The Testament of Reuben 3 says the same, "he no longer touched her" (Charles). Genesis tells the cost to Reuben instead: "you will not be first, because you went up onto your father's bed" (Genesis 49:4), and Chronicles explains that "his birthright went to the sons of Israel's son Joseph" (1 Chronicles 5:1).

a: They must surely die together
p: Leviticus 20:11: "The two of them must be put to death."
b: "A man who lies with his father's wife has exposed his father's nakedness. The two of them must be put to death" (Leviticus 20:11). Jubilees says this law was already written on the heavenly tablets, and that Reuben's story is why Moses must teach it. Leviticus 18:8 gives the ban without a penalty; Leviticus 20:11 gives the penalty.

a: Cursed is anyone who lies with his father's wife
p: Deuteronomy 27:20, but in Deuteronomy the people say Amen. Here the Lord's holy ones do.
b: Deuteronomy 27:20: "A curse on anyone who has sex with his father's wife, for he has lifted the wing of his father's cloak!" And all the people will say, "Amen!" Differs: in Jubilees the holy ones, the angels, answer "So be it, so be it" (Ge'ez läykun läykun, "let it be"). The law is shown as agreed in heaven before Israel ever said it. "Written a second time" seems to mean that the law stands twice in the Torah, in Leviticus and Deuteronomy.

a: it carries the sentence of death
p: Ge'ez kʷənäne mot, a Hebrew legal phrase also found in Jeremiah 26:16.
b: Charles traces kʷənäne mot to Hebrew mishpat mavet, the phrase the officials use when they say Jeremiah "does not deserve a death sentence" (Jeremiah 26:16).

a: stoned with stones
p: Leviticus does not say how. Jubilees and the Mishnah both say stoning.
b: Leviticus 20:11 says "put to death" without naming the means. Jubilees says stoning. So does the Mishnah, which lists among "those who are stoned to death" one who lies "with his father's wife, even if she is not his mother" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:4). Here Jubilees and the later rabbis agree on how to apply the law.

a: Let no one say
t: Why was Reuben not put to death?
p: The book's own answer: the full law had not yet been revealed. Others denied that he sinned.
b: Readers of Genesis asked why Reuben lived and kept his place among the twelve. Jubilees: the law and its penalty had not yet been revealed "in full for everyone" (33:16), so Reuben was spared; now that Moses has it, there is no forgiveness. Some rabbis: he never did it. "Anyone who says that Reuben sinned with Bilhah is nothing other than mistaken"; he only moved his father's bed out of Bilhah's tent for his mother Leah's sake (Talmud, Shabbat 55b, in the Davidson English). The same page records that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua held that he did sin.

a: had not been revealed in full for everyone
p: Charles: the book here anticipates Paul, "where there is no law, there is no transgression."
b: Jubilees says the patriarchs kept laws already on the heavenly tablets, but that this law, with its penalty, was revealed "in full" only to Moses. Charles saw here an anticipation of Romans 4:15, "transgression does not exist where there is no law." Compare Romans 5:13: "with no law there, sin is not counted." Differs: Paul uses the idea to show that the law brings awareness of sin and anger; Jubilees uses it to defend the fathers and to make the law stricter now.

a: In your days it is revealed
p: The Ge'ez has no verb here. "It is revealed" is supplied from the start of the verse.
b: Word for word the Ge'ez says, "for in your days, as a law of time in its days." Charles also supplies "(it has been revealed)," in brackets. "Your" means Moses, to whom the angel speaks.

a: not sin a sin that brings death
p: The phrase 1 John uses for sin one should not pray about.
b: The Ge'ez says "sin a sin of death." 1 John 5:16 says, "There is sin headed toward death. I am not saying he should make a request about that." In Jubilees it means a sin whose penalty is death in the law. Readers of 1 John differ on what John meant; see the notes there. Charles links this verse with 21:22.

a: He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe
p: Words from Deuteronomy 10:17, which Paul repeats about the Jew and the Greek.
b: "He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17). Paul applies the first half to Jews and Gentiles alike: "For with God there are no favorites" (Romans 2:11). Jubilees means that not even a patriarch's son would escape this law now.

a: the sexual sin they commit
p: Ge'ez zəmmut covers every forbidden sexual act. Jubilees calls it the greatest sin.
b: The Ge'ez word (here "than fornication," ʾəmzəmuna) covers sexual sin of every kind; Charles translates "fornication." Jubilees ranks it above every other sin because it defiles a people meant to be holy. Paul too sets it apart: "the person who sins sexually is sinning against his own body" (1 Corinthians 6:18), but he does not call it the greatest sin.

a: a nation of priests, a kingdom of priests
p: Exodus 19:6, which 1 Peter and Revelation apply to the church.
b: God told Israel at Sinai, "you will be for me a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6). 1 Peter gives the titles to the church, "a royal priesthood, a holy nation" (1 Peter 2:9), and so does Revelation 1:6. The Latin of Jubilees has populus sacerdotalis et regalis, "a priestly and royal people" (Charles).

a: Jacob's only daughter
p: Genesis 37:35 speaks of "all his daughters." Jubilees says Dinah was the only one.
b: Matches Genesis 35:23–26 in the list of sons. Settles a question: Genesis names only Dinah (Genesis 30:21; 46:15) but says "all his sons and all his daughters came to comfort him" (Genesis 37:35). Jubilees calls Dinah "Jacob's only daughter," and in 34:14 the comforters are "his sons and his daughter."

a: Seven kings of the Amorites
p: Jacob says he took land "from the Amorites with my sword and my bow." This is that war.
b: In Genesis 48:22 Jacob tells Joseph, "I give one shoulder of land, which I took from the Amorites with my sword and my bow." Genesis tells no such battle. Charles thought Jubilees kept an old legend of Jacob's conquest around Shechem, told more fully in the Testament of Judah 3–7 and in medieval Hebrew retellings (the Midrash Wayissa'u). Differs from Genesis 34, where Jacob takes no part in the attack on Shechem and blames Simeon and Levi.

a: the king of Tafu
p: Charles identified most of the names: Tappuah, Hazor, Shiloh, Gaash, Beth-horon, Mahanaim.
b: Charles's identifications: Tafu is Tappuah, Tephon in 1 Maccabees; Ares is a corruption of Hazor; Seragan is Sartan in the Hebrew retellings; Selo is Shiloh; Gaaz may be Gaash, the hill country where Joshua was buried (Joshua 24:30); Betoron is Beth-horon; Maanisakir is a corrupt form of "Shakir of Mahanaim." Several are places where the Maccabees fought or that their enemies fortified: Bacchides "built strong towns in Judea ... Beth-horon ... Timnath ... and Tephon" (1 Maccabees 9:50).

a: He killed Ares, Tafu, Seragan, Selo, Maanisakir and Gaaz.
p: The Ge'ez spells several names differently here; Betoron is missing.
b: In this list the Ge'ez has Saregan, Silo, Amanisakir and Gagaas; the Plain English Translation uses the spellings of 34:4 so the reader can follow. The king of Betoron is not named, so six of the seven die. Charles notes that the Testament of Judah 4 also has six kings killed. The names stand for the kings, as in the Ge'ez.
orig: ወለሰሬጋን ፡ ወለሲሎ ፡ ወለአማኒሰኪር ፡ ወለጋጋአስ (wäläsäregan wäläsilo wäläʾämanisäkir wälägagaʾäs)

a: He built Robel and Tamnatares
p: Probably Arbela and Timnath-heres. Judah says, "I built Timnah and my father Rabahel."
b: Charles took Robel as a corruption of Arbela, the stronghold Bacchides took (1 Maccabees 9:2), and Tamnatares as Timnath-heres, where Joshua was buried (Judges 2:9), the Timnath that Bacchides fortified (1 Maccabees 9:50). The Testament of Judah 7 has Judah say, "I built Timnah, and my father Rabahel" (Charles's quotation).
r: Judges 2:9; 1 Maccabees 9:2; 1 Maccabees 9:50; Testament of Judah 7

a: the land of Dothan
p: Genesis 37:12–17, told in one verse. The Ge'ez name is Dotaim.
b: Genesis has Jacob send Joseph to "find out how your brothers are doing" (Genesis 37:14), and Joseph finds them at Dothan (Genesis 37:17). The Ge'ez spells the place Dotaim. Jubilees dates the sending to the seventh year of the week. Genesis says Joseph was seventeen (Genesis 37:2), and so does Jubilees at 39:2.

a: Then they changed their minds and sold him to Ishmaelite traders
p: Jubilees leaves out the pit, Reuben's rescue plan, Judah's speech and the Midianites.
b: Matches Genesis on the plot and the sale (Genesis 37:18–28). Shortens: there is no pit, no Reuben trying to save Joseph, no Judah asking "What is the profit if we kill our brother?" (Genesis 37:26), and no Midianites. The brothers act as one, which suits the confession and fasting of 34:18–19.

a: Pharaoh's eunuch, the chief of the cooks
p: Genesis says "a court official ... who commanded the bodyguard." Jubilees, like the Septuagint, has "chief cook."
b: Genesis 37:36 calls Potiphar seris parʿoh sar ha-ṭabbaḥim. Saris can mean "eunuch" but often just "court official." Ṭabbaḥ means "slaughterer": a cook, or an executioner, so "commander of the bodyguard." Charles notes that Jubilees and the Septuagint both took it as "chief cook," and that "eunuch" need not be taken literally here.
orig: ለኅፅወ ፡ ፈርዖን ፡ ሊቀ ፡ መብስላን (läḫḍəwä färʿon liqä mäbsəlan)

a: priest of the city of Elew
p: Jubilees joins Joseph's master to Asenath's father, the priest of On (Heliopolis).
b: Joseph later marries "Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On" (Genesis 41:45). Jubilees makes Potiphar himself the priest. Elew is the Greek name Heliopolis, "city of the sun," the Septuagint's name for On (Charles). Genesis keeps the two men apart.

a: on the tenth of the seventh month
p: The day the bloody robe reached Jacob is the date of the Day of Atonement.
b: The tenth of the seventh month is the Day of Atonement: "On the tenth day of the seventh month you are to humble yourselves" (Leviticus 16:29). Jubilees dates the brothers' lie to that very day, and in 34:18–19 explains the fast by it.

a: An evil beast has eaten Joseph
p: Jacob's cry in Genesis 37:33.
b: "My son's robe! ... A wild beast has eaten him. Joseph is torn, torn to pieces!" (Genesis 37:33). The Ge'ez has ʾärwe ḍäwag, "an evil beast," like the King James Version's "an evil beast hath devoured him." Jubilees adds that Jacob grew feverish and that the robe came in the evening, so he mourned all night.

a: So these three griefs came on Israel in one month
p: Genesis does not tell their deaths. Jubilees adds both to Jacob's grief over Joseph.
b: Goes beyond: Genesis never says how or when Bilhah or Dinah died. Jubilees has both die in the month Joseph was lost, so Jacob grieves three times over. Later Jewish writers gave Dinah other stories: in Genesis Rabbah 80 she marries Simeon (Charles notes it).

a: Qafratef
p: Charles: perhaps a corrupt "Eder of Ephrath," or the same as Kabratan in 32:32.
b: Charles suggests two explanations: a corruption of "Eder of Ephrath" (see 33:1), or another form of Kabratan (32:32), near Bethlehem. Either would put Bilhah near Rachel's tomb, where she is buried (34:16). His manuscript c reads Qaratifa.

a: Let me go down to the grave mourning for my son
p: Genesis 37:35. Jubilees adds that his mourning lasted a year.
b: "He said, 'No, I will go down to my son in Sheol, still mourning'" (Genesis 37:35). The Ge'ez has "the grave" (mäqabr) where the Hebrew has Sheol, the place of the dead.

a: That is why it is ordained for the Israelites to afflict themselves
t: Why the Day of Atonement? Jubilees answers
p: Leviticus 16 gives the rite but no story. Jubilees ties the fast to the brothers' sin against Jacob.
b: Matches: the date, "the tenth day of the seventh month," the fasting, the goat, "once a year," and "for all their sins" all come from Leviticus 16:29–34. Goes beyond: Leviticus gives no event in Israel's past as the reason. Jubilees makes the Day remember the sons of Jacob, who "grieved their father's tender love" by selling Joseph and lying about it. Charles notes that the rabbinic tradition knows nothing of this origin. Leviticus also has two goats, one for the LORD and one for Azazel (Leviticus 16:8–10); Jubilees names one.

a: afflict themselves
p: Leviticus' "humble yourselves." Both mean going without food.
b: Leviticus 16:29 says "you are to humble yourselves," Hebrew teʿannu et-nafshotekhem, which the site translates "humble yourselves." Charles notes that the phrase is the technical term for fasting (compare Ezra 8:21; Daniel 10:12). The Ge'ez yəḥmämu means "be afflicted, suffer."

a: with a young goat
t: Claude's theory: a goat for a goat
p: The brothers deceived Jacob with a goat's blood (34:12). Israel atones with a goat.
b: Claude's observation: the same Ge'ez word, ṭäli (goat), stands in 34:12, where the brothers kill "a young male goat" and dip the robe in its blood, and here, where Israel makes atonement "with a young goat" on the same date. The writer seems to have set the two goats side by side: the animal of the lie becomes the animal of atonement.

a: cleanse themselves on this day once a year
p: Hebrews reads the yearly Day as a sign that the old sacrifices could not end sin.
b: Leviticus 16:30: "on this day atonement will be made for you, to make you clean." Hebrews draws a different lesson from the yearly repeat: "in these sacrifices sins are called to mind year after year" (Hebrews 10:3), and Christ entered once for all (Hebrews 9:7–12). The Mishnah adds that the Day atones for sins against God, but for sins against another person only "until he appeases the other person" (Mishnah Yoma 8:9): a rule that fits a fast born from wrong done to a father.

a: Adebaa, a Canaanite
t: A Canaanite wife, against the book's own law
p: Genesis 46:10 says Simeon's son Shaul was born to "a Canaanite woman." Jubilees keeps it.
b: Matches Genesis 46:10 and Exodus 6:15: "Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman." Jubilees forbids marriage to Canaanites in the strongest terms (30:7–17), yet it does not explain the fact away. Charles credits the author for this; later rabbis did explain it away, for example by making Shaul Dinah's son (Genesis Rabbah 80; Charles notes it). In 34:21 Simeon "changed his mind" and took a wife from Mesopotamia.

a: Betasuel, a Canaanite
p: The name comes from Hebrew bat-shua, "the daughter of Shua" (Genesis 38:2).
b: Genesis 38:2 says Judah married "the daughter of a Canaanite man whose name was Shua." The Hebrew bat-shuaʿ became a personal name, Betasuel here and Bathshua in other texts; the Testament of Judah has it too (Charles). Charles adds that some copies of Targum Onqelos changed "Canaanite" to "merchant," to soften it.

a: Melka, one of the daughters of Aram
p: Genesis names none of these wives. A Syriac list gives nearly the same names.
b: Genesis names only Asenath (Genesis 41:45). Nearly the same names are found in a Syriac list of the patriarchs' wives drawn from Jubilees, which Charles printed in his edition of the Ethiopic text. The Testament of Levi 11 also calls Levi's wife Melcha. "Terah" is Ge'ez Taran. Levi marries within Abraham's family, as the book wants.

a: [Neeman]
p: The square brackets mark a doubtful name: VanderKam prints it in brackets with a question mark.
b: VanderKam's Ge'ez text gives Zebulun's wife's name in brackets with a question mark. Charles marks the name with daggers as doubtful and notes that his manuscripts a, b and d leave it out, so it "may be the invention of an Ethiopic scribe"; the Syriac list of the wives has "Adni" instead. The Plain English Translation keeps the name in brackets, so that the doubt shows in the line (see the variant).

a: Simeon changed his mind
p: The Ge'ez verb means to turn back or repent.
b: Tämäyṭä means "turn back, return, repent." Charles translates "Simeon repented." The writer counts Simeon's first marriage as a fault he put right.

a: he was to honor them all the days of his life
p: The fifth commandment, applied by a mother to her son, and stretched to his brother.
b: "Honor your father and your mother, so that your days will stretch out long" (Exodus 20:12). Rebekah adds the brother. Jubilees keeps telling the fathers obeying laws before Sinai.

a: I have seen the day of my death in a dream
p: Genesis never tells of Rebekah's death. Jubilees gives her a farewell and an age, 155.
b: Goes beyond: Genesis says only, "There they buried Isaac and his wife Rebekah" (Genesis 49:31). Jubilees gives her a dream, last words, and an age that matches 35:27: three jubilees (147 years), a week (7) and a year make 155. In Jubilees, as in Genesis 25:23, God's plan for the brothers is first told to Rebekah.

a: her teeth were strong
p: Like Moses at 120: "his vigor had not drained away."
b: "His eyesight had not grown weak, and his vigor had not drained away" (Deuteronomy 34:7). Rebekah, too, dies with her strength. Jacob's laugh recalls Sarah laughing at a word about the future (Genesis 18:12).

a: Make Esau swear that he will not harm Jacob
p: George Syncellus quotes this scene in Greek, crediting it to Josephus by mistake.
b: The Byzantine chronicler George Syncellus gives this passage in Greek, naming Josephus at the start and Jubilees at the end. As Charles prints it: "Rebekah asked Isaac in his old age to exhort Esau and Jacob to love one another. And having exhorted them he foretold that if Esau should rise against Jacob, he would fall into his hands." Charles judged that Syncellus wrongly credited it to Josephus.

a: He has taken your flocks for himself
p: Genesis tells nothing like this. It is part of the book's harsh picture of Esau.
b: Goes beyond: in Genesis Esau has his own great wealth and moves away from Jacob (Genesis 36:6–8). Jubilees has him strip his parents while Jacob is in Haran, and Rebekah says there is "no goodness in him."

a: he acted like a man doing us a kindness
p: Rebekah's bitter irony: he handed back their own goods as if they were a gift.
b: Word for word: "he makes himself like a man who pities us." Asked for what was theirs, Esau behaved as if he were being generous.

a: I used to love Esau more than Jacob
p: Genesis says "Isaac loved Esau." Jubilees has Isaac turn to Jacob before he dies.
b: "Isaac loved Esau, because he had a taste for game, but Rebekah loved Jacob" (Genesis 25:28). Goes beyond: Genesis never says Isaac changed. Jubilees has him say he loved Esau first only as the firstborn, and now loves Jacob more. The prophets put it in God's mouth: "Jacob I loved. But Esau I hated" (Malachi 1:2–3), which Paul quotes about God's choosing (Romans 9:13).

a: injustice and violence
p: The Ge'ez pair 1 Enoch uses for the wicked.
b: ʿämäḍa wägfəʿ is the pair the site renders "injustice" and "violence" in 1 Enoch 91–108, where it names the deeds of the wicked. Applied to Esau, it makes him the type of the violent sinner.

a: he has left the God of Abraham and gone after his wives
p: Genesis says Esau's Hittite wives were "a bitterness of spirit." Jubilees makes them lead him to idols.
b: Genesis: Esau's wives "were a bitterness of spirit to Isaac and to Rebekah" (Genesis 26:35), and Rebekah dreads a Hittite wife for Jacob (Genesis 27:46). Goes beyond: Jubilees says Esau followed their "uncleanness" and "error" and left Abraham's God. This is the danger of marriage outside Israel that the whole book warns against (25:1–10; 30:7–17).

a: for he will fall into his hands
p: Charles thought this last clause a later addition repeating what came before.
b: The verse already says Esau "will be handed over into Jacob's hands." Charles marked "for he will fall into his hands" as a gloss, a note that slipped into the text. The Ge'ez verb means "go down": Esau will go down into Jacob's power. It looks ahead to 38:2.
orig: እስመ ፡ ውስተ ፡ እዴሁ ፡ ይወርድ (ʾəsmä wəstä ʾədehu yəwärd)

a: Jacob's guardian is great, mighty and honored
t: Jacob's guardian: an angel, or God?
p: Charles took it as the earliest clear mention of a person's guardian angel. It may mean God himself.
b: ʿäqabi means "keeper, guardian." Guardian angel: Charles called this "the earliest distinct reference" to the belief that each person has a guardian angel, and compared Matthew 18:10 ("their angels in heaven"), Acts 12:15 ("It is his angel") and Hebrews 1:14. Daniel 10 gives nations their angelic princes. God himself: God promised Jacob, "I will guard you everywhere you go" (Genesis 28:15), and the words "great, mighty, honored" fit God. On this reading Esau's guardian would be a lesser power. The Ge'ez allows both.
r: Genesis 28:15; Matthew 18:10; Acts 12:15; Hebrews 1:14; Daniel 10:13; Daniel 10:20–21

a: bury me near Sarah, your father's mother
p: Genesis 49:31 says Rebekah was buried in Machpelah. Here Esau promises it.
b: "There they buried Isaac and his wife Rebekah" (Genesis 49:31). Jubilees gives Esau the task, and in 35:27 both sons bury her.

a: We were sown together in your body
p: Esau speaks of their birth in Genesis 25, where the twins already fought.
b: "The children crushed against each other inside her" (Genesis 25:22), and "two peoples will divide from your body" (Genesis 25:23). Esau now makes their shared birth the reason to love. Hosea remembers the struggle: "While still in the womb, he caught his brother's heel" (Hosea 12:3).

a: he will surely be king over me and my sons
p: Esau accepts Isaac's blessing of Jacob: "Be master over your brothers."
b: Isaac told Jacob, "Be master over your brothers" (Genesis 27:29), and Esau, "your brother you will serve" (Genesis 27:40). The oracle at their birth said, "the elder will serve the younger" (Genesis 25:23). Here Esau says it himself, which makes his later war (chapters 37–38) a breaking of his own word.

a: I will be first in nothing except love
p: Jacob, who took the firstborn's place, promises to be first in love alone.
b: The quarrel of the twins was over who would be first. Jacob turns the word around. Paul's advice is close: "Each of you be first to honor the other" (Romans 12:10).

a: the double cave
p: The Ge'ez translates the name Machpelah, from a Hebrew root meaning "double."
b: Genesis calls the tomb "the cave of the field of Machpelah" (Genesis 23:19). The Hebrew name is from the root for "double," and the Ge'ez says "the cave of the two" (bäʾät zäʾnətä kəlʾe). The book uses the name for the tomb of Sarah, Rebekah, Isaac and Leah (36:2; 36:21).

a: the eternal house
p: Ecclesiastes 12:5 calls the grave the house of forever.
b: Charles compares Ecclesiastes 12:5, "the human is on his way to his house of forever," Hebrew bet ʿolamo. The Ge'ez bet zäläʿaläm is the same phrase.

a: In the tomb I dug for myself
p: In Genesis it is Jacob who says "my grave, the one I dug for myself."
b: Joseph reports his father's words: "Bury me in my grave, the one I dug for myself in the land of Canaan" (Genesis 50:5). Jubilees puts the same wish in Isaac's mouth, one of many ways it makes the fathers' lives echo each other.

a: do what is right and upright on the earth
p: God chose Abraham so he would teach his children "what is right and fair."
b: "I have chosen him so that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the LORD's way by doing what is right and fair. Then the LORD can bring about for Abraham all that he has said about him" (Genesis 18:19). Isaac's testament follows the same order: do right, so that the Lord will do what he promised.

a: love your brothers as a man loves his own soul
p: Leviticus 19:18, and Jonathan's love for David.
b: "You are to love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18). Jonathan "loved him as much as his own life" (1 Samuel 18:1). Jesus calls the Leviticus command the second greatest (Matthew 22:39), and 1 John says, "Everyone who hates his brother is a killer" (1 John 3:15): a line that fits the end of this story.

a: About idols
p: Jacob made his household bury their foreign gods (Genesis 35:2–4). Isaac warns his sons the same way.
b: "Put away the foreign gods in your midst" (Genesis 35:2). Abraham's warnings against idols run through Jubilees (12; 20–22). Here Isaac warns both sons, though in 35:14 he has said that Esau has already gone after his wives' gods.

a: the plant of righteousness
p: A name for Israel shared with 1 Enoch, and close to Isaiah's "Oaks of Righteousness."
b: Täklä ṣədq is the phrase the site renders "the plant of righteousness" in 1 Enoch (10:16; 93:2–10), where it means the faithful people God plants forever. Isaiah calls the restored people "Oaks of Righteousness, / the LORD's planting" (Isaiah 61:3).

a: by the name that is glorious and honored
p: Isaac makes his sons swear by God's name. Jesus later says, "do not take oaths at all."
b: Matches: the Torah allows oaths by God's name (Deuteronomy 6:13; 10:20), and the fathers swear often in Genesis. Differs: Jesus says, "do not take oaths at all" (Matthew 5:34), and James repeats it (James 5:12). Churches differ on what Jesus' words forbid; see "Where Christians differ" at Matthew 5:34. The broken oath is the hinge of the next chapter (37:17).

a: will fall into his hand
p: Isaac's warning is fulfilled when Jacob kills Esau (38:2).
b: Isaac does not name Esau, but the reader knows. In 35:16 he told Rebekah the same. The story of 37–38 shows the oath broken and the warning fulfilled.

a: as he burned Sodom
p: The fire of Genesis 19 as the picture of final judgment.
b: "Then the LORD rained sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah" (Genesis 19:24). Moses warned that a land that turns to other gods will be "like the overthrow of Sodom" (Deuteronomy 29:23), and Jude makes Sodom "an example" of eternal fire (Jude 7).

a: the book of life
p: Names in the book of life, or in the book of those who perish.
b: Moses asks God to "wipe me out ... from your book" (Exodus 32:32); the psalm prays, "Let them be wiped out of the scroll of life" (Psalm 69:28); Revelation says, "I will never erase his name from the book of life" (Revelation 3:5). Charles notes that Jubilees also has a book of destruction, the opposite of the book of life, and compares the "books of wrath" of 1 Enoch 39:2.

a: the book of the instruction of humankind
p: An unusual name. It seems to mean the record of those who are taught and corrected.
b: Mäṣḥäfä tägśaṣä säbʾ: tägśaṣ means teaching, correction or discipline. Charles translates "the book of the discipline of the children of men." It seems to name the record of people who live under God's teaching.

a: the one who was born first
p: Esau was born first, but sold his birthright. So who is "the one born first" here?
b: Read alone, 36:12–13 sounds as if Isaac gives the larger share to Esau, the elder twin. Esau then says he sold the birthright to Jacob, "Let it be given to him" (36:14), and 37:1 says Isaac gave it to Jacob. Charles's chapter heading takes the larger share as Jacob's. Some read "the one born first" as a legal title that passed to Jacob when he bought it (Genesis 25:33); others read Isaac as offering it to Esau, who refuses.

a: the Well of the Oath
p: Ge'ez "well of the oath" translates the meaning of Beersheba.
b: "That is why the place was called Beersheba, because there the two of them swore an oath" (Genesis 21:31). Beer means "well" and sheba can mean "oath." The Ge'ez gives the meaning, not the name.

a: larger share greater
p: The Ge'ez verb means "make great." Charles emended to "I will give."
b: The Ge'ez has ʾäʿäbi, "I make great." Charles thought it a copying slip for ʾəhub, "I will give" (see the variant). The Plain English Translation keeps the Ge'ez: the firstborn's share is the larger one, and Isaac enlarges it.

a: the Lord Most High
p: Charles counted how often writers used "Most High" and found it most common in the 100s BC.
b: Charles listed the title "Most High" across Jewish writings: frequent in Jubilees, forty-eight times in Sirach and thirteen in Daniel, he counted, but rare in the Prophets and in the century after. He took the frequency as one sign of the book's date in the second century BC.

a: he slept the eternal sleep
p: Genesis 35:28 gives the same age. Its own numbers put the death after Joseph was sold, as here.
b: Matches: "Isaac lived a hundred and eighty years" (Genesis 35:28). Genesis tells the death in chapter 35, before Joseph's story, but its numbers place it later: Isaac was 60 at Jacob's birth (Genesis 25:26), so he died when Jacob was 120; Jacob was 130 when he met Pharaoh (Genesis 47:9), after seven good years and two years of famine had passed since Joseph rose to power at thirty (Genesis 41:46; 45:6), so Joseph was sold when Jacob was about 108. Jubilees tells it in that order. "Slept the eternal sleep" is also found in the Testaments of Dan and Issachar (Charles).

a: by the commands that had been made known
p: Charles: the commands shown to Jacob on the seven tablets (32:21).
b: The Ge'ez has "according to the commands that appear"; the Latin, "according to the visible commands, according to the division of the times of his generations" (Charles). Charles explains that the commands "were made visible to Jacob on the seven tablets which the angel showed him," the tablets of 32:21, with the future of his family set out by its time divisions.

a: he never heard a harsh word from her mouth
p: Genesis remembers Leah as "the unloved one." Jubilees ends her life with Jacob's love.
b: "The LORD saw that Leah was the unloved one" (Genesis 29:31). Goes beyond: Genesis never says Jacob came to love her, though he chose to be buried beside her: "there I buried Leah" (Genesis 49:31). Jubilees says that after Rachel died he loved her "with all his heart," and gives her a praise like that of the capable wife of Proverbs 31.

a: Esau's sons heard that Isaac had given the birthright to Jacob
t: A war Genesis does not tell
p: Genesis ends the twins' story in peace. Jubilees ends it with war and Esau's death.
b: Conflicts in spirit: in Genesis, Esau runs to meet Jacob and "they wept" (Genesis 33:4), and the two bury Isaac together (Genesis 35:29); Esau then moves to Seir (Genesis 36:6–8). Genesis never tells how Esau died. The law later says, "Do not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother" (Deuteronomy 23:7), and forbids Israel to fight Esau's descendants on the way to Canaan (Deuteronomy 2:4–5). Goes beyond: Jubilees adds a war in which Jacob kills Esau. Charles thought the story an ancient legend, also known to the Testament of Judah 9.

a: for a little lentil stew
p: Esau tells his own story fairly: he sold it (Genesis 25) and was tricked (Genesis 27).
b: "Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil stew ... So Esau despised the birthright" (Genesis 25:34). Hebrews says he "sold his own birthright" for one meal (Hebrews 12:16). Esau then speaks of the stolen blessing: "Your brother came with trickery and took your blessing" (Genesis 27:35). Charles notes how favorably this chapter treats Esau himself; the blame falls on his sons.

a: You are putting your neck under his yoke
p: Isaac told Esau he would one day "tear his yoke off your neck." His sons want that day now.
b: "By your sword you will live, / and your brother you will serve. / But when you break loose, / you will tear his yoke off your neck" (Genesis 27:40). Esau's sons try to break the yoke and fail: in 38:12 Jacob's sons put "the yoke of servitude" on them.

a: Aduram, their father's friend
t: Aduram: a man and a place
p: Here a man, in 38:3 "Aduran the Aramean," in 38:8 a place. Charles: Adoraim in Idumea.
b: The Ge'ez name ʾAduram is a person here, "the friend of their father," and in 38:3 Aduran the Aramean is killed by Jacob's second arrow. In 38:8–9 it is the hill where Esau falls. Charles identifies the place with Adoraim (Adora), a town of Idumea; the Latin has Adurin and the Testament of Judah 9 Adoram. The Yalkut makes Aduran an Edomite (Charles).

a: from the Kittim
p: The Horites were Seir's first people. The Kittim were a people of the western coasts (Genesis 10:4).
b: Genesis names "Seir the Horite, the people who lived in the land" (Genesis 36:20). The Kittim were first the people of Cyprus (Genesis 10:4); Balaam foresees "ships ... from the coast of Kittim" (Numbers 24:24), and Daniel 11:30 says "ships from Kittim will sail against him."

a: He was filled with wrath and fury
p: Esau resists at first. His sons threaten him, then his old hatred returns.
b: Charles stressed that Jubilees, unlike later Jewish retellings, blames Esau's sons more than Esau: he refuses, warns them, and goes only under threat of death (37:7–11). Then he "remembered all the evil that had lain hidden in his heart" (37:13). The writer allows Esau a struggle, but in the end his heart, not his sons, decides.

a: He was mourning his wife Leah
t: The same story in the Yalkut
p: A medieval Hebrew collection tells the attack during the mourning for Leah, with 4,000 men.
b: Charles quotes the Yalkut Shimoni: "It was the year when Leah died and Jacob and his sons were mourning ... Then came (Esau) against them with a mighty army ... 4000 warriors," who surrounded the tower where Jacob and his sons had gathered. The Hebrew tradition knew the same story, and Charles judged Jubilees' form the oldest.

a: What a fine comfort you have come to comfort me with
p: Ge'ez "good is the comfort": Jacob's irony at a brother who comes armed to a funeral.
b: Word for word: "good is the comfort you have come to comfort me with." Esau comes with an army during Jacob's mourning, so Jacob's "fine comfort" is sarcasm. Then he names the broken oath (35:24).

a: If the boar changes its skin
p: In 1 Enoch's Animal Apocalypse Esau is a boar. Esau calls himself one here.
b: Esau's sayings are like Jeremiah's: "Can a Cushite change his skin, / or a leopard its spots?" (Jeremiah 13:23). The boar is Esau's animal: in the Animal Apocalypse the boar stands for Esau and Edom (1 Enoch 89:12; Charles), and Psalm 80:13 has "A wild hog from the woods" ravaging Israel's vine. In 37:24 Jacob sees him charge "like the boar."

a: The breasts were parted from their mother
p: A damaged line? Charles thought these words were out of place, and meant "since the twins left their mother."
b: The line does not fit the animal sayings around it. Charles suggested that it belongs after 37:19 and that a few letters had been miscopied, giving: "for you have not been a brother to me since the twins were separated from their mother." As it stands, the Ge'ez seems to say that the bond of the womb is broken. Charles's manuscript d has "I shall not be a brother to you" (see the variant).

a: if the wolves make peace with the lambs
p: Esau names as impossible what Isaiah promises for the day of the Messiah.
b: Contrasts: "The wolf will stay as a guest with the lamb" and "the lion, like the ox, will eat straw" (Isaiah 11:6–7; compare Isaiah 65:25). For Isaiah these are signs of the coming king's peace. Esau uses the same pictures to say peace will never come.

a: the raza
p: A large white bird, Charles says from an Amharic dictionary. Dillmann thought it meant rice.
b: Charles explains raza from Isenberg's Amharic dictionary as "a large white bird which eats grasshoppers"; Dillmann had taken it as "rice." The saying needs a white bird: when the black raven turns white, Esau will love his brother.

a: like the boar that runs onto the spear
p: A hunter's picture: the boar charges so hard it drives itself onto the spear.
b: A wild boar was hunted with a spear held fast; the charging animal ran onto it. Esau's charge will kill him, as Isaac said: "whoever plans evil against his brother will fall into his hand" (36:9).

a: He is close to you and like you
p: Judah says the sons will not kill their uncle. Esau's death must come from his equal.
b: Judah's reason is honor: Esau is Jacob's twin, "close to you and like you," and his sons will not raise a hand against him. Charles, with the Latin, read the last words as "let us give him (this) honor" (see the variant). In the Yalkut, Judah instead asks how long Jacob will keep speaking of peace (Charles).

a: brought him down
p: Genesis never tells Esau's death. Here Jacob shoots him. Later tradition named another killer.
b: Goes beyond, and conflicts in spirit: Genesis leaves the twins at peace, and the story of a brother killing a brother recalls Cain (Genesis 4:8). Esau had planned to kill Jacob (Genesis 27:41); here the plan turns back on him. The Testament of Judah 9 also says, "Jacob struck Esau with a bow." Later Jewish tradition gave the deed to Hushim son of Dan at Jacob's burial (Targum Pseudo-Jonathan on Genesis 50:13; Sotah 13a; Charles notes both).

a: dividing themselves on the four sides of the tower
t: Four sides, as in the Yalkut
p: The Hebrew Yalkut tells the sally from the tower in the same order, side by side.
b: Charles quotes the Yalkut: "Judah went forth first and Naphtali and Gad with him to the south of the tower, and 50 servants ... And Levi and Dan and Asher went forth on the east ... Reuben and Issachar and Zebulon ... on the north ... Simeon and Benjamin and Enoch the son of Reuben ... on the west." The match is exact, so a Hebrew form of this story survived among Jews into the Middle Ages.

a: Hanoch, Reuben's son
p: The Ge'ez has Enoch. Genesis 46:9 spells Reuben's son Hanoch: the same Hebrew name.
b: "The sons of Reuben: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron and Carmi" (Genesis 46:9). The Hebrew Ḥanokh is the name English Bibles spell Enoch in Genesis 5 and Hanoch here. The Ge'ez writes ʾEnok; the Plain English Translation uses Genesis' spelling for Reuben's son.

a: on the hill in Aduram
p: Charles: Adora, one of the Idumean towns John Hyrcanus took. A clue to the writer's time.
b: Charles identified Aduram with Adora (Adoraim), a town of Idumea, the land of the Edomites south of Judea. Josephus says that John Hyrcanus "took also Dora and Marissa, cities of Idumea, and subdued all the Idumeans," letting them stay if they would be circumcised and live by the laws of the Jews (Antiquities 13.9.1, Whiston's English). For Charles this placed the book under Hyrcanus. Others date it earlier and see an older legend here (see the book's opening pages).

a: But Jacob buried his brother
p: Even in war Jacob buries Esau. In the Yalkut his sons bury him for their father's sake.
b: Leaving an enemy unburied was a disgrace. Jacob buries his brother where he fell. Charles quotes the Yalkut: the sons of Jacob "found Esau's dead body and they buried it out of respect for their father." The Testament of Judah 9 says he died at a place it calls Anoniram (Charles).

a: put the yoke of servitude on them
p: Isaac's word, "your brother you will serve," fulfilled. David later did the same.
b: "Your brother you will serve" (Genesis 27:40). Under David "every Edomite became David's servant" (2 Samuel 8:14), and Balaam foretold, "Edom will become his property" (Numbers 24:18). The Testament of Judah 9 says Edom gave "two hundred kor of wheat" until Jacob's family went down to Egypt (Charles quotes the Greek).
r: Genesis 27:40; 2 Samuel 8:14; Numbers 24:18; Testament of Judah 9

a: to this day
p: Genesis says Esau would one day break the yoke, and Kings says Edom did. Jubilees says it never did.
b: Conflicts: Isaac told Esau, "when you break loose, / you will tear his yoke off your neck" (Genesis 27:40), and Kings records that "Edom revolted out from under Judah's hand ... down to this day" (2 Kings 8:20–22). Jubilees says Edom has not escaped "to this day." Charles read the line against the writer's own time, when Edom was made subject to Judea by John Hyrcanus (see 38:8).

a: These are the kings who reigned in Edom
p: Jubilees places Genesis 36:31–39 here, after Edom is subdued.
b: "These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the people of Israel" (Genesis 36:31). Jubilees adds "to this day" and sets the list after Edom's defeat, so the kings of Edom rule a people already serving Jacob. The words "before any king reigned over" Israel look ahead to the time of Israel's kings.

a: Balak son of Beor
p: Genesis has Bela son of Beor and Dinhabah. Jubilees' forms are close to the Septuagint's.
b: Genesis 36:32: "Bela son of Beor reigned in Edom. The name of his city was Dinhabah." Charles compares each name with the Hebrew and the Septuagint and finds Jubilees nearer the Greek: Balak (Greek Balak), Danaba (Greek Dennaba). A son of Beor named Balak brings to mind Balak king of Moab and Balaam son of Beor (Numbers 22:5).

a: Adat son of Bard
p: Genesis 36:35: "Hadad son of Bedad, who struck down Midian in the country of Moab."
b: The Hebrew has Hadad son of Bedad, and his city Avith. The Ge'ez Adat for Hadad and Bard for Bedad follow forms close to the Greek (Charles). The other names in the list match Genesis the same way: Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah, Husham from the land of the Temanites (Genesis 36:33–34).

a: Saloman from Emaseqa
p: Genesis 36:36. Charles gives the Greek forms Salama and Marekka.
b: "Hadad died, and Samlah from Masrekah reigned in his place" (Genesis 36:36). Charles lists the Septuagint's Salama and Marekka beside the Ge'ez Saloman and Emaseqa. The next two kings match Genesis 36:37–38: Shaul from Rehoboth on the River, Baal-hanan son of Achbor.

a: Maytabit daughter of Matrit, daughter of Metabedzaab
t: The last king and his wife
p: Genesis 36:39 has Hadar, his city Pau, and Mehetabel daughter of Matred, daughter of Me-zahab.
b: "Baal-hanan son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his place. The name of his city was Pau, and his wife's name was Mehetabel daughter of Matred, daughter of Me-zahab" (Genesis 36:39). Jubilees leaves out the city and has Adat for Hadar, like the Greek Arath that Charles cites. Charles gives the Greek of the wife's name as Metebeel.
